In the 1950s the French firm Selmer and the American firm Gibson brought out standard, reverb and concert models; Harald Bode developed a six-octave transposing version, licensed for manufacture by Jørgensen Electronics of Germany. The Univox of the British Jennings Organ Company was inspired by it, and in 1962 a prototype based on the clavioline also appeared in Japan. In the 1960s it was liked, along with the Mellotron, by rock and pop keyboard players, and until the Moog synthesiser arrived it was an important keyboard instrument.

Its sound is set by the square-wave tone of a valve oscillator and, after filtering, comes out neither warm nor fully dark but neutral. Its range covers three octaves, and it cuts through strongly, with a real presence in a mix. The built-in tremolo gives the sound a slight wobble, an organ-like pulsing that is nonetheless sharper and more synthetic than a traditional pipe organ. Where a piano resonates naturally, the clavioline's sound comes entirely from amplified circuitry; beside an electronic organ its timbre has more of the raw electronic flavour of its period.

The clavioline is an electrophonic keyboard instrument invented in 1947 in Versailles by the French engineer Constant Martin, Hornbostel–Sachs 531.1. It consists of a keyboard with a separate amplifier and speaker, usually of about three octaves, with switches that change the timbre and add tremolo and other effects; it sounds through a valve oscillator producing a buzz close to a square wave, shaped by high- and low-pass filtering and by distortion in the amplifier. In the 1960s rock and pop musicians used it often in recordings and films, and France, the United States, Germany, Britain and Japan all produced or derived related electronic keyboards.
